headline: A 65-Fold Options Trade on Intel Raises Insider-Trading Questions
lede: On May 8, 2026, an anonymous trader turned $34,000 into $2.22 million in roughly fifteen minutes holding Intel call options set to expire that day — purchased when they were nearly worthless — apparently before the Wall Street Journal reported that Apple and Intel had struck a preliminary chip-manufacturing deal. The position multiplied sixty-five-fold as Intel shares rocketed to an intraday high of $130.57, up roughly 17% from the day's open. On financial social media, the trade was flagged with a sarcastic disclaimer: “Clearly not an insider.”
body:
The mechanics are straightforward, if extreme. Intel (INTC) opened May 8 at $111.81, already up nearly 70% from its April 23 close of $66.78 after the company’s first-quarter earnings — revenue of $13.6 billion, non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.29 against a near-zero analyst consensus — triggered the stock’s best single-day gain since 1987. The $120 call options expiring that same day were roughly $8 *out-of-the-money* and priced in pennies, reflecting near-zero probability of finishing in the money by market close. When the *Wall Street Journal* story on the Apple (AAPL)–Intel chip deal broke intraday, the stock surged roughly 17% from its opening price in minutes, reaching a peak of $130.57 before closing at $124.92. At that intraday peak, each $120 call carried $10.57 of **intrinsic value** — the difference between the stock price and the *strike*, the fixed price at which the holder can buy shares. A position sold at around a $126 stock price would produce exactly the reported $2.22 million from a $34,000 stake.

The return profile is legally recognizable. A trader who buys out-of-the-money short-dated calls on a company’s stock hours before a major corporate announcement, then exits at a 65-fold gain as that announcement breaks, is exhibiting the precise pattern the Securities and Exchange Commission’s *ARTEMIS* system — the Advanced Relational Trading Enforcement Metrics Investigation System — was built to detect. ARTEMIS holds roughly ten billion equity and options trade records and can identify the same account trading ahead of multiple unrelated corporate events over time. FINRA, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, generates more than 450 insider-trading referrals to the SEC annually from its own continuous market surveillance.

Recent enforcement history makes the pattern concrete. In April 2024, a federal jury found Matthew Panuwat liable for *shadow trading* — he purchased out-of-the-money calls in Incyte (INCY) seven minutes after receiving an internal email announcing his employer’s acquisition by Pfizer, betting the news would lift a correlated oncology peer. At Kaman Corporation (2025), three individuals pleaded guilty to trading call options before an acquisition announcement, with illicit profits exceeding $1 million. A 2024 lawyer insider-trading ring built its strategy explicitly around “out-of-the-money call options bought just before deal announcements,” communicating in coded language to obscure the scheme. In each case the tell was the same: improbably profitable options positions established in the narrow window before a market-moving event.

The underlying deal warrants context. According to the *Wall Street Journal*, Apple (AAPL) and Intel (INTC) had reached a preliminary agreement for *Intel Foundry* — Intel’s contract chip-manufacturing division, positioning the company as a Western alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) — to produce chips for Apple devices. The U.S. government, which holds an equity stake in Intel, reportedly facilitated negotiations that had been ongoing for more than a year. No formal deal has been confirmed by either company. The announcement is strategically significant: Apple has long been Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing’s most important customer, and a shift of even a fraction of its orders to Intel Foundry would validate Intel’s costly bet on domestic advanced manufacturing.

Whether the trader had advance knowledge is unknown — the identity is not public. “Clearly not an insider” is a recognized trope on *FinTwit*, financial social media, a winking acknowledgment of a suspiciously timed trade that functions simultaneously as a brag and a provocation. It carries no legal weight. The SEC traces accounts, not declarations of innocence made in ironic tweets. The trade may have been a remarkable coincidence — a retail speculator who bought the right lottery ticket on the right morning. But the pattern is precisely what surveillance systems exist to flag, and precision is exactly what those systems are good at.

concepts.definition: Zero Days to Expiration options are contracts that expire at the end of the trading session in which they are purchased. Because there is no time value left, they are priced almost entirely on the probability that the underlying stock will finish above (for calls) or below (for puts) the strike price by market close. A stock move that pushes through the strike on expiration day can produce extreme percentage returns because the initial premium is so cheap.

A call option is out-of-the-money when the underlying stock price is below the option’s strike price, meaning the option has no intrinsic value and would expire worthless if the stock stays where it is. The further OTM an option is, the cheaper its premium — but the more dramatic the percentage gain if the stock moves through the strike.

The fixed price at which an options contract gives the holder the right to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying stock. A $120 call gives the holder the right to buy Intel shares at $120 regardless of the market price; that right is valuable only if the market price exceeds $120 before or at expiration.

For a call option, intrinsic value is the amount by which the stock price exceeds the strike price. A $120 call on a stock trading at $130 has $10 of intrinsic value. On expiration day, intrinsic value is essentially all an in-the-money option is worth, since there is no time remaining for further movement.

The SEC’s Advanced Relational Trading Enforcement Metrics Investigation System — a database of roughly ten billion equity and options trade records. It ranks transactions by suspicion level and can identify the same trader placing well-timed bets across multiple unrelated corporate events over years, making it the primary algorithmic tool for detecting repeat insider trading in options markets.

The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, the self-regulatory body that oversees U.S. broker-dealers and their registered personnel. FINRA operates its own market surveillance systems and submits hundreds of insider-trading referrals to the SEC each year based on anomalous trading patterns it detects across all U.S. securities markets.

A form of insider trading in which someone uses material non-public information about one company to trade securities of a related or correlated company — for example, trading a competitor’s options after learning about an acquisition at one’s own employer. Established as legally actionable by the SEC in SEC v. Panuwat, where a jury found the defendant liable in April 2024.

Intel’s contract chip-manufacturing division (formerly Intel Foundry Services, or IFS), which aims to produce semiconductors for external customers on Intel’s advanced process nodes, including 18A and 14A. It is Intel’s bid to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing as a Western, domestically-rooted alternative, supported in part by U.S. government subsidies and strategic interest.

Financial Twitter — the community of traders, analysts, and commentators who share market observations and trade ideas on X (formerly Twitter). “Clearly not an insider” is a recognized FinTwit sarcasm trope used when a trade looks suspiciously well-timed relative to a subsequent market-moving announcement; it functions simultaneously as a brag and a wink at regulators.
